section.heading: 8. Calculus of Several Variables
Introduction
section.paragraph: Up to now, we have dealt with functions involving one variable. However, many situations involve functions of two or more variables. For example, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) compiled by the Bureau of Labor Statistics depends on the price of more than $$95,000$$ consumer items. To study such relationships, we need the notion of a function of several variables, the first topic in this chapter. Next, generalizing the concept of the derivative of a function of one variable, we study the partial derivatives of a function of two or more variables. Using partial derivatives, we study the rate of change of a function with respect to one variable while holding all other variables constant. We then learn how to find the extremum values of a function of several variables. As an application of optimization theory, we learn how to find an equation of the straight line that “best” fits a set of data points scattered about a straight line. We also extend the concept of the differential of one variable, which was introduced in Section 3.7, to the case of a function of two or more variables. Finally, we generalize the notion of the integral to the case involving a function of two variables.

section.heading: Functions of Two Variables
section.paragraph: Although this chapter deals with real-valued functions of several variables, most of our definitions and results are stated in terms of a function of two variables. One reason for adopting this approach, as you will soon see, is that there is a geometric interpretation for this special case, which serves as an important visual aid. We can then draw upon the experience gained from studying the two-variable case to help us understand the concepts and results connected with the more general case, which, by and large, is just a simple extension of the lower-dimensional case.

note.title: A Function of Two Variables
note.heading: A Function of Two Variables
note.paragraph: A real-valued function of two variables $$f$$ consists of

list.item: A set $$A$$ of ordered pairs of real numbers $$(x,y)$$ called the domain of the function.
A rule that associates with each ordered pair in the domain of $$f$$ one and only one real number, denoted by $$z = f(x,y)$$ .

section.paragraph: The variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are called independent variables, and the variable $$z$$ , which is dependent on the values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , is referred to as a dependent variable.

As in the case of a real-valued function of one real variable, the number $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ is called the value of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at the point $$({x,y})$$ . And, unless specified, the domain of the function $$f$$ will be taken to be the largest possible set for which the rule defining $$f$$ is meaningful.

section.heading: Graphs of Functions of Two Variables
section.paragraph: To graph a function of two variables, we need a three-dimensional coordinate system. This is readily constructed by adding a third axis to the plane Cartesian coordinate system in such a way that the three resulting axes are mutually perpendicular and intersect at O. Observe that, by construction, the zeros of the three number scales coincide at the origin of the three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system (Figure 3).

section.paragraph: Now, if $$f{({x,y})}$$ is a function of two variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ , the domain of $$f$$ is a subset of the $$xy$$ -plane. If we denote $$f{({x,y})}$$ by $$z$$ , then the totality of all points $$({x,y,z})$$ , that is, $$({x,y,f{({x,y})})}$$ , makes up the graph of the function $$f$$ and is, except for certain degenerate cases, a surface in three-dimensional space (Figure 5).

section.paragraph: In interpreting the graph of a function $$f{({x,y})}$$ , one often thinks of the value $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ of the function at the point $$({x,y})$$ as the “height” of the point $$({x,y,z})$$ on the graph of $$f$$ . If $$f(x,y) > 0$$ , then the point $$({x,y,z})$$ is $$f{({x,y})}$$ units above the $$xy$$ -plane; if $$f(x,y) < 0$$ , then the point $$({x,y,z})$$ is $$\left| f(x,y) \right|$$ units below the $$xy$$ -plane.

section.heading: Level Curves
section.paragraph: We can visualize the graph of a function of two variables by using level curves. To define the level curve of a function $$f$$ of two variables, let $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ and consider the trace of $$f$$ in the plane $$z = k$$ ( $$k$$ , a constant), as shown in Figure 7a. If we project this trace onto the $$xy$$ -plane, we obtain a curve $$C$$ with equation $$f{({x,y})} = k$$ , called a level curve of $$f$$ (Figure 7b).

note.title: Level Curves
note.heading: Level Curves
note.paragraph: The level curves of a function $$f$$ of two variables are the curves with equations $$f(x,y) = k$$ , where $$k$$ is a constant in the range of $$f$$ .

section.paragraph: Notice that the level curve with equation $$f{({x,y})} = k$$ is the set of all points in the domain of $$f$$ corresponding to the points on the surface $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ having the same height or depth $$k$$ . By drawing the level curves corresponding to several admissible values of $$k$$ , we obtain a contour map. The map enables us to visualize the surface represented by the graph of $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ : We simply lift or depress the level curve to see the “cross sections” of the surface. section.paragraph: Level curves of functions of two variables are found in many practical applications. For example, if $$f{({x,y})}$$ denotes the temperature at a location within the continental United States with longitude $$x$$ and latitude $$y$$ at a certain point in time, then the temperature at the point $$({x,y})$$ is given by the “height” of the surface, represented by $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ . In this situation, the level curve $$f{({x,y})} = k$$ is a curve superimposed on a map of the United States, connecting points having the same temperature at a given time (Figure 11). These level curves are called isotherms.

image.alt: The map of USA, divided into many zones by curves representing different temperature zones.

figure.caption: Isotherms: curves connecting points that have the same temperature

section.paragraph: Similarly, if $$f{({x,y})}$$ gives the barometric pressure at the location $$({x,y})$$ , then the level curves of the function $$f$$ are called isobars, lines connecting points having the same barometric pressure at a given time.

As a final example, suppose $$P{({x,y,z})}$$ is a function of three variables $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ that gives the profit realized when $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ units of three products, $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ , respectively, are produced and sold. Then, the equation $$P{({x,y,z})} = k$$ , where $$k$$ is a constant, represents a surface in three-dimensional space called a level surface of $$P$$ . In this situation, the level surface represented by $$P{({x,y,z})} = k$$ represents the product mix that results in a profit of exactly $$k$$ dollars. Such a level surface is called an isoprofit surface.

section.heading: 8.2. Partial Derivatives
Partial Derivatives
section.paragraph: For a function $$f(x)$$ of one variable $$x$$ , there is no ambiguity when we speak about the rate of change of $$f(x)$$ with respect to $$x$$ , since $$x$$ must be constrained to move along the $$x$$ -axis. The situation becomes more complicated, however, when we study the rate of change of a function of two or more variables. For example, the domain $$D$$ of a function of two variables $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a subset of the plane, so if $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ is any point in the domain of $$f$$ , there are infinitely many directions from which one can approach the point $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ (Figure 12). We may therefore ask for the rate of change of $$f$$ at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ along any of these directions.

image.alt: Details A point with coordinate (a, b) is plotted in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. Four arrows from the top, the right, the bottom left, the top left points toward the point (a, b).

figure.caption: We can approach a point in the plane from infinitely many directions.

section.paragraph: However, we will not deal with this general problem. Instead, we will restrict ourselves to studying the rate of change of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ at a point $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ in each of two preferred directions—namely, the direction parallel to the $$x$$ -axis and the direction parallel to the $$y$$ -axis. Let $$y = b$$ , where $$b$$ is a constant, so that $$f\left( {x,b} \right)$$ is a function of the one variable $$x$$ . Since the equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is the equation of a surface, the equation $$z = f\left( {x,b} \right)$$ is the equation of the curve $$C$$ on the surface formed by the intersection of the surface and the plane $$y = b$$ (Figure 13).

A perpendicular is dropped from a point (a, b, f (a, b)) to the edge of the plane in the x y plane at a point (a, b).

section.paragraph: Because $$f\left( {x,b} \right)$$ is a function of one variable $$x$$ , we may compute the derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ at $$x = a$$ . This derivative, obtained by keeping the variable $$y$$ fixed at $$b$$ and differentiating the resulting function $$f\left( {x,b} \right)$$ with respect to $$x$$ , is called the first partial derivative of $$\mathbf{f}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , written
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
or
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
or
$$f_{x}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
Thus,

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\left( {a,b} \right) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\left( {a,b} \right) = f_{x}\left( {a,b} \right) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {a + h,b} \right) - f\left( {a,b} \right)}{h}$$

provided that the limit exists. The first partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ measures both the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the curve $$C$$ and the rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$x$$ -direction when $$x = a$$ and $$y = b$$ . We also write
$$\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right|_{(a,b)} = f_{x}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
Similarly, we define the first partial derivative of $$\mathbf{f}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{y}$$ at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , written
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
or
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
or
$$f_{y}\left( {a,b} \right)$$
as the derivative obtained by keeping the variable $$x$$ fixed at $$a$$ and differentiating the resulting function $$f\left( {a,y} \right)$$ with respect to $$y$$ . That is,

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\left( {a,b} \right)} = {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\left( {a,b} \right) = f_{y}\left( {a,b} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\left( {a,b} \right)} = {\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {a,b + k} \right) - f\left( {a,b} \right)}{k}}} \end{array}$$

if the limit exists. The first partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$y$$ at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ measures both the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the curve $$C$$ , obtained by holding $$x$$ constant (Figure 14), and the rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$y$$ -direction when $$x = a$$ and $$y = b$$ . We write
$$\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right|_{({a,b})} = f_{y}\left( {a,b} \right)$$

section.paragraph: For an economic interpretation of the first partial derivatives of a function of two variables, let’s turn our attention to the function

where $$a$$ and $$b$$ are positive constants with $$0 < b < 1$$ . This function is called the Cobb–Douglas production function . Here, $$x$$ stands for the amount of money expended for labor, $$y$$ stands for the cost of capital equipment (buildings, machinery, and other tools of production), and the function $$f$$ measures the output of the finished product (in suitable units) and is called, accordingly, the production function.

The partial derivative $$f_{x}$$ is called the marginal productivity of labor . section.heading: Substitute and Complementary Commodities
section.paragraph: For another application of the first partial derivatives of a function of two variables in the field of economics, let’s consider the relative demands of two commodities. We say that the two commodities are substitute (competitive) commodities if a decrease in the demand for one results in an increase in the demand for the other. Examples of substitute commodities are coffee and tea. Conversely, two commodities are referred to as complementary commodities if a decrease in the demand for one results in a decrease in the demand for the other as well. Examples of complementary commodities are automobiles and automobile tires.

We now derive a criterion for determining whether two commodities $$A$$ and $$B$$ are substitute or complementary. Suppose the demand equations that relate the quantities demanded, $$x$$ and $$y$$ , to the unit prices, $$p$$ and $$q$$ , of the two commodities are given by
and

Let’s consider the partial derivative $$\partial f \slash \partial p$$ . Since $$f$$ is the demand function for Commodity $$A$$ , we see that for fixed $$q$$ , $$f$$ is typically a decreasing function of $$p$$ —that is, $$\partial f \slash \partial p < 0$$ . Now, if the two commodities were substitute commodities, then the quantity demanded of Commodity $$B$$ would increase with respect to $$p$$ —that is, $$\partial g \slash \partial p > 0$$ . A similar argument with $$p$$ fixed shows that if $$A$$ and $$B$$ are substitute commodities, then $$\partial f \slash \partial q > 0$$ . Thus, the two commodities $$A$$ and $$B$$ are substitute commodities if
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q} > 0$$
and
$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} > 0$$
Similarly, $$A$$ and $$B$$ are complementary commodities if
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q} < 0$$
and
$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} < 0$$

section.heading: 8.3. Maxima and Minima of Functions of Several Variables
Maxima and Minima
section.paragraph: In Chapter 4, we saw that the solution of a problem often reduces to finding the extreme values of a function of one variable. In practice, however, situations also arise in which a problem is solved by finding the absolute maximum or absolute minimum value of a function of two or more variables.

For example, suppose Scandi Company manufactures computer desks in both assembled and unassembled versions. Its profit $$P$$ is therefore a function of the number of assembled units, $$x$$ , and the number of unassembled units, $$y$$ , manufactured and sold per week; that is, $$P = f(x,y)$$ . A question of paramount importance to the manufacturer is: How many assembled and unassembled desks should the company manufacture per week to maximize its weekly profit? Mathematically, the problem is solved by finding the values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ that will make $$f(x,y)$$ a maximum.

In this section, we will focus our attention on finding the extrema of a function of two variables. As in the case of a function of one variable, we distinguish between the relative (or local) extrema and the absolute extrema of a function of two variables.

note.source_type: Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables
note.title: Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables
note.heading: Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on a region $$R$$ containing the point $$({a,b})$$ . Then $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$({a,b})$$ if $$f{({x,y})} \leq f(a,b)$$ for all points $$({x,y})$$ that are sufficiently close to $$({a,b})$$ . The number $$f(a,b)$$ is called a relative maximum value . Similarly, $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$({a,b})$$ , with relative minimum value $$f(a,b)$$ , if $$f{({x,y})} \geq f(a,b)$$ for all points $$({x,y})$$ that are sufficiently close to $$({a,b})$$ .

section.paragraph: Loosely speaking, $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$({a,b})$$ if the point $$({a,b,f(a,b)})$$ is the highest point on the graph of $$f$$ when compared with all nearby points. A similar interpretation holds for a relative minimum.

If the inequalities in this last definition hold for all points $$({x,y})$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , then $$f$$ has an absolute maximum (or absolute minimum ) at $$({a,b})$$ with absolute maximum value (or absolute minimum value ) $$f(a,b)$$ . Figure 16 shows the graph of a function with relative maxima at $$({a,b})$$ and $$({e,g})$$ and a relative minimum at $$({c,d})$$ . The absolute maximum of $$f$$ occurs at $$({e,g})$$ , and the absolute minimum of $$f$$ occurs at $$({h,i})$$ .

Now let’s turn our attention to the study of relative extrema of a function. Suppose that a differentiable function $$f(x,y)$$ of two variables has a relative maximum (relative minimum) at a point $$({a,b})$$ in the domain of $$f$$ . and
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}{({a,b})}$$
must be zero.

section.paragraph: To summarize, a function $$f$$ of two variables can have a relative extremum only at a point $$({a,b})$$ in its domain where $$\partial f \slash \partial x$$ and $$\partial f \slash \partial y$$ both exist and are equal to zero at $$({a,b})$$ or at least one of the partial derivatives does not exist. As in the case of one variable, we refer to a point in the domain of $$f$$ that may give rise to a relative extremum as a critical point. The precise definition follows.

note.title: Critical Point of f
note.heading: Critical Point of f
note.paragraph: A critical point of $$f$$ is a point $$({a,b})$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that both
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}{({a,b})} = 0$$
and
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}{({a,b})} = 0$$
or at least one of the partial derivatives does not exist.

section.paragraph: To determine the nature of a critical point of a function $$f(x,y)$$ of two variables, we use the second partial derivatives of $$f$$ . The resulting test, which helps us to classify these points, is called the second derivative test and is incorporated in the following procedure for finding and classifying the relative extrema of $$f$$ .

list.item: Find the critical points of $$f(x,y)$$ by solving the system of simultaneous equations $$\begin{array}{l} {f_{x}{({x,y})} = 0} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})} = 0} \end{array}$$

The second derivative test: Let $$D\left( {x,y} \right) = f_{xx}\left( {x,y} \right)f_{yy}\left( {x,y} \right) - f_{xy}^{2}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ Then $$D{({a,b})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({a,b})} < 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative maximum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . $$D{({a,b})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({a,b})} > 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . $$D{({a,b})} < 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . The point $$({a,b,f(a,b)})$$ is called a saddle point. $$D{({a,b})} = 0$$ implies that the test is inconclusive, so some other technique must be used to solve the problem.

section.paragraph: As in the case of a practical optimization problem involving a function of one variable, the solution to an optimization problem involving a function of several variables calls for finding the absolute extremum of the function. Determining the absolute extremum of a function of several variables is more difficult than merely finding the relative extrema of the function. However, in many situations, the absolute extremum of a function actually coincides with the largest relative extremum of the function that occurs in the interior of its domain. We assume that the problems considered here belong to this category. Furthermore, the existence of the absolute extremum (solution) of a practical problem is often deduced from the geometric or practical nature of the problem.

The Method of Least Squares
section.paragraph: In Section 1.4, Example 10, we saw how a linear equation can be used to approximate the sales trend for a local sporting goods store. As we saw there, one use of a trend line is to predict a store’s future sales. Recall that we obtained the line by requiring that it pass through two data points, the rationale being that such a line seems to fit the data reasonably well.

In this section, we describe a general method, known as the method of least squares , for determining a straight line that, in some sense, best fits a set of data points when the points are scattered about a straight line. section.heading: 8.5. Constrained Maxima and Minima and the Method of Lagrange Multipliers
Constrained Relative Extrema
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3, we studied the problem of determining the relative extrema of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ without placing any restrictions on the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ —except, of course, that the point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lie in the domain of $$f$$ . Such a relative extremum of a function $$f$$ is referred to as an unconstrained relative extremum of $$f$$ . However, in many practical optimization problems, we must maximize or minimize a function in which the independent variables are subjected to certain further constraints.

In this section, we discuss a powerful method for determining the relative extrema of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ whose independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are required to satisfy one or more constraints of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ . Such a relative extremum of a function $$f$$ is called a constrained relative extremum of $$f$$ . We can see the difference between an unconstrained extremum of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ of two variables and a constrained extremum of $$f$$ , where the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are subjected to a constraint of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ , by considering the geometry of the two cases. Figure 26a depicts the graph of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ that has an unconstrained relative minimum at the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . However, when the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are subjected to an equality constraint of the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ , the points $$(x,y,z)$$ that satisfy both $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ lie on a curve $$C$$ . Therefore, the constrained relative minimum of $$f$$ must also lie on $$C$$ (Figure 26b).

section.paragraph: The major drawback of the technique used in Example 1 is that it relies on our ability to solve the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ for $$y$$ explicitly in terms of $$x$$ . This is not always easy. Moreover, even when we can solve the constraint equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ for $$y$$ explicitly in terms of $$x$$ , the resulting function of one variable that is to be optimized may turn out to be unnecessarily complicated. Fortunately, an easier method exists. This method, called the method of Lagrange multipliers (Joseph Lagrange, 1736–1813), is as follows:

section.paragraph: Recall that if $$f$$ is a function of one variable defined by $$y = f(x)$$ , then the increment in $$y$$ is defined to be
$$\Delta y = f\left( {x + \Delta x} \right) - f(x)$$

where $$\Delta x$$ is an increment in $$x$$ (Figure 30a). The increment of a function of two or more variables is defined in an analogous manner. For example, if $$z$$ is a function of two variables defined by $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , then the increment in $$z$$ is
$$\Delta z = f\left( {x + \Delta x,y + \Delta y} \right) - f\left( {x,y} \right)$$
where $$\Delta x$$ and $$\Delta y$$ are the increments in the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ , respectively. (See Figure 30b.)

note.title: Total Differential
note.heading: Total Differential
note.paragraph: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ define a differentiable function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ .

list.item: The differentials of the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are $$dx = \Delta x$$ and $$dy = \Delta y$$ .
The differential of the dependent variable $$z$$ is (17) $$dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy$$

section.paragraph: Thus, analogous to the one-variable case, the total differential of $$z$$ is a linear function of $$dx$$ and $$dy$$ . Furthermore, it provides us with an approximation of the exact change in $$z$$ ,
$$\Delta z = f\left( {x + \Delta x,y + \Delta y} \right) - f\left( {x,y} \right)$$
corresponding to a net change $$\Delta x$$ in $$x$$ from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ and a net change $$\Delta y$$ in $$y$$ from $$y$$ to $$y + \Delta y$$ ; that is,
$$\Delta z \approx dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\left( {x,y} \right)dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\left( {x,y} \right)dy$$
provided that $$\Delta x = dx$$ and $$\Delta y = dy$$ are sufficiently small.

note.title: Applied Example 5. Error Analysis
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Error Analysis
note.paragraph: Find the maximum percentage error in calculating the volume of a rectangular box if an error of at most $$1\%$$ is made in measuring the length, width, and height of the box.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ denote the length, width, and height, respectively, of the rectangular box. Then the volume of the box is given by $$V = f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xyz$$ cubic units. Now suppose that the true dimensions of the rectangular box are $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ units, respectively. Since the error committed in measuring the length, width, and height of the box is at most $$1\%$$ , we have

$$\begin{matrix} {\left| {\Delta x} \right| = {\left| {x - a} \right| \leq 0.01a}} \\ {\left| {\Delta y} \right| = {\left| {y - b} \right| \leq 0.01b}} \\ {\left| {\Delta z} \right| = {\left| {z - c} \right| \leq 0.01c}} \end{matrix}$$
Therefore, the maximum error in calculating the volume of the box is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx {|{dV}| = \left| {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}dz} \middle| \right|_{x = a,y = b,z = c}}} \\ \left. \phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|} = \middle| yzdx + xzdy + xydz \middle| \right|_{x = a,y = b,z = c} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{= \left| {bcdx + acdy + abdz} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{\leq bc\left| {dx} \right| + ac\left| {dy} \right| + ab\left| {dz} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{\leq bc\left( {0.01a} \right) + ac\left( {0.01b} \right) + ab\left( {0.01c} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{= (0.03)abc}} \end{array}$$
Since the actual volume of the box is $$abc$$ cubic units, we see that the maximum percentage error in calculating its volume is
$$\frac{\left| {\Delta V} \right|}{\left. V \right|_{({a,b,c})}} \approx \frac{(0.03)abc}{abc} = 0.03$$
that is, approximately $$3\%$$ .

section.heading: 8.7. Double Integrals
A Geometric Interpretation of the Double Integral
section.paragraph: To introduce the notion of the integral of a function of two variables, let’s first recall the definition of the definite integral of a continuous function of one variable $$y = f(x)$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . We first divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals, each of equal length, by the points $$x_{0} = a < x_{1} < x_{2} < \cdots < x_{n} = b$$ and define the Riemann sum by
$$S_{n} = f\left( p_{1} \right)h + f\left( p_{2} \right)h + \cdots + f\left( p_{n} \right)h$$

where $$h = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ and $$p_{i}$$ is an arbitrary point in the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ . The definite integral of $$f$$ over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is then defined as the limit of the Riemann sum $$S_{n}$$ as $$n$$ tends to infinity, whenever it exists. Furthermore, recall that when $$f$$ is a nonnegative continuous function on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then the $$i$$ th term of the Riemann sum, $$f\left( p_{i} \right)h$$ , is an approximation (by the area of a rectangle) of the area under that part of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = x_{i - 1}$$ and $$x = x_{i}$$ , so that the Riemann sum $$S_{n}$$ provides us with an approximation of the area under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ . The integral
$$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}S_{n}}$$
gives the actual area under the curve from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ .

Now suppose $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a continuous function of two variables defined over a region $$R$$ . For simplicity, we assume for the moment that $$R$$ is a rectangular region in the plane (Figure 32). Let’s construct a Riemann sum for this function over the rectangle $$R$$ by following a procedure that parallels the case for a function of one variable over an interval $$I$$ . We begin by observing that the analog of a partition in the two-dimensional case is a rectangular grid composed of $$\mathit{mn}$$ rectangles, each of length $$h$$ and width $$k$$ , as a result of partitioning the side of the rectangle $$R$$ of length $$\left( {b - a} \right)$$ into $$m$$ segments and the side of length $$\left( {d - c} \right)$$ into $$n$$ segments. By construction,
$$h = \frac{b - a}{m}$$
and
$$k = \frac{d - c}{n}$$

section.paragraph: Let’s label the rectangles $$R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}\ldots.,R_{\mathit{mn}}$$ . If $$\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ is any point in $$R_{i}\left( {1 \leq i \leq mn} \right)$$ , then the Riemann sum of $$\mathbf{f}\left( {\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \right)$$ over the region $$\mathbf{R}$$ is defined as
$$S\left( {m,n} \right) = f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)hk + f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)hk + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( {x_{\mathit{mn}},y_{\mathit{mn}}} \right)hk$$

If the limit of $$S\left( {m,n} \right)$$ exists as both $$m$$ and $$n$$ tend to infinity, we call this limit the value of the double integral of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over the region $$R$$ and denote it by
$$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

If $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a nonnegative function, then it defines a solid $$S$$ bounded above by the graph of $$f$$ and below by the rectangular region $$R$$ . Furthermore, the solid $$S$$ is the union of the $$\mathit{mn}$$ solids bounded above by the graph of $$f$$ and below by the $$\mathit{mn}$$ rectangular regions corresponding to the partition of $$R$$ (Figure 34).

section.heading: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Plane Region
section.paragraph: Up to now, we have assumed that the region over which a double integral is to be evaluated is rectangular. In fact, however, it is possible to compute the double integral of functions over rather arbitrary regions. The next theorem, which we state without proof, expands the number of types of regions over which we may integrate.

section.paragraph: Suppose the plane region $$R$$ represents a certain district of a city and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives the population density (the number of people per square mile) at any point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ . section.heading: Average Value of a Function
section.paragraph: In Section 6.5, we showed that the average value of a continuous function $$f(x)$$ over an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is given by

That is, the average value of a function over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is the integral of $$f$$ over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ divided by the length of the interval. An analogous result holds for a function of two variables $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over a plane region $$R$$ . To see this, we enclose $$R$$ by a rectangle and construct a rectangular grid. Let $$\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ be any point in the rectangle $$R_{i}$$ of area $$hk$$ . Now, the average value of the $$mn$$ numbers $${f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)},{f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)},\ldots,{f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)}$$ is given by
$$\frac{f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right) + f\left( {x_{2,}y_{2}} \right) + \cdots + f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)}{mn}$$
which can also be written as

$$\begin{matrix} {\frac{hk}{hk}\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right) + f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right) + \cdots + f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)}{mn} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{1}{\left( {mn} \right)hk}\left\lbrack {f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right) + f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right) + \cdots + f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)} \right\rbrack hk} \end{matrix}$$

Now the area of $$R$$ is approximated by the sum of the $$mn$$ rectangles (omitting those having no points in common with $$R$$ ), each of area $$hk$$ . Note that this is the denominator of the previous expression. Therefore, taking the limit as $$m$$ and $$n$$ both tend to infinity, we obtain the following formula for the average value of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over $$R$$ .

list.item: The domain of a function $$f$$ of two variables is a subset of the $$xy$$ -plane. The rule of $$f$$ associates with each ordered pair in the domain of $$f$$ one and only one real number, denoted by $$z =$$ $$f{({x,y})}$$ .

If the function $$f$$ has rule $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , then $$x$$ and $$y$$ are called independent variables, and $$z$$ is a/an dependent variable. The number $$z$$ is also called the value of $$f$$ at $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

The graph of a function $$f$$ of two variables is the set of all points $$(x,y,z)$$ , where $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ and $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is the domain of $$f$$ . The graph of a function of two variables is a/an surface in three-dimensional space.

The trace of the graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in the plane $$z = k$$ is the curve with equation $$f(x,y) = k$$ lying in the plane $$z = k$$ . The projection of the trace of $$f$$ in the plane $$z = k$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane is called the level curve of $$f$$ . The contour map associated with $$f$$ is obtained by drawing the level curves of $$f$$ corresponding to several admissible values of $$k$$ .

The partial derivative $$\partial f \slash \partial x$$ of $$f$$ at $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ can be found by thinking of $$y$$ as a/an constant in the expression for $$f$$ and differentiating this expression with respect to $$x$$ as if it were a function of $$x$$ alone.

The number $$f_{x}\left( {a,b} \right)$$ measures the slope of the tangent line to the curve $$C$$ obtained by intersecting the graph of $$f$$ with the plane $$y = b$$ at the point $$(a,b,f(a,b))$$ . It also measures the rate of change of $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ at the point $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ with $$y$$ held fixed with value $$b$$ .

A function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ has a relative maximum at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\leq$$ $$f\left( {a,b} \right)$$ for all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ that are suffiently close to $$(a,b)$$ . The absolute maximum value of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is the number $$f\left( {a,b} \right)$$ such that $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\leq$$ $$f\left( {a,b} \right)$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in the domain of $$f$$ .

A critical point of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a point $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that $$f_{x}(a,b) = 0$$ and $$f_{y}(a,b) = 0$$ or at least one of the partial derivatives of $$f$$ does not exist. A critical point of $$f$$ is a/an candidate for a relative extremum of $$f$$ .

By plotting the points associated with a set of data, we obtain the scatter diagram for the data. The least-squares line is the line obtained by minimizing the sum of the squares of the errors made when the $$y$$ -values of the data points are approximated by the corresponding $$y$$ -values of the least-squares line. The least-squares equation is found by solving the normal equations.

The method of Lagrange multipliers solves the problem of finding the relative extrema of a function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ subject to the constraint $$g(x,y) = 0$$ . We first form the Lagrangian function $$F\left( {x,y,\lambda} \right) =$$ $$f(x,y) + \lambda g(x.y)$$ . Then we solve the system consisting of the three equations $$F_{x} = 0$$ , $$F_{y} = 0$$ , and $$F_{\lambda} = 0$$ for $$x,y$$ , and $$\lambda$$ . These solutions give the critical points that give rise to the relative extrema of $$f$$ .

For a differentiable function $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , the differentials of the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are $$dx = \Delta x$$ and $$dy = \Delta y$$ , and the differential of the dependent variable $$z$$ is $$dz =$$ $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy$$ .

If $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is continuous and nonnegative over a region $$R$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane and $$\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)\mathit{dA}}}$$ exists, then the double integral gives the volume of the solid bounded by the graph of $$f(x,y)$$ over the region $$R$$ .

The integral $$\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)\mathit{dA}}}$$ is evaluated by using iterated integrals. For example, $$\int_{R}{\int{\left( {2x + y^{2}} \right)dA}}$$ , where $$R = \left\{ (x,y) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;3 \leq y \leq 5 \right\}$$ , is equal to $${\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{3}^{5}\left( 2x + y^{2} \right)}}dydx$$ or the (iterated) integral $${\int_{3}^{5}{\int_{0}^{1}{(2x + y^{2})}}}dxdy$$ .
